chunks.arabic_text: رِجَالُ الْكَشِّيِّ: مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ قُلْوَيْهَ، عَنْ سَعْدٍ، عَنْ أَحْمَدَ بْنِ مُحَمَّدٍ، عَنِ الْحُسَيْنِ بْنِ سَعِيدٍ، عَنْ مُعْمَرَ بْنِ خَلَّادَ قَالَ

translations.en: Rijal al-Kashshi: Muhammad ibn Qulawayh, from Sa'd, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muammar ibn Khallad who said:

chunks.arabic_text: أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامِ قَالَ: مَا ذِئْبَانِ ضَارِيَانِ فِي غَنَمٍ قَدْ غَابَ عَنْهَا رُعَاؤُهَا بِأَضَرَّ فِي دِينِ الْمُسْلِمِ مِنْ حُبِّ الرِّيَاسَةِ، ثُمَّ قَالَ: لَكِنَّ صَفْوَانَ لَا يُحِبُّ الرِّيَاسَةَ

translations.en: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: Two ravenous wolves set loose in a flock of sheep whose shepherd is absent are not more dangerous to a Muslim's religion than the love of leadership (desire for prominence/rulership). Then he said: But Safwan does not love leadership.

en.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) employs the vivid metaphor of two ravenous wolves in an unguarded flock to illustrate how the love of leadership (ri'asah) devours a Muslim's religion. He specifically applies this teaching to his companion Safwan ibn Yahya, noting that while he held high status, he was free from this spiritual danger. This hadith highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on internal purity of intention over external rank, a key theme in the biographies of the Imams' close companions.
en.seo_question: What is the spiritual danger of loving leadership according to Imam al-Rida?

key_terms.الرِّيَاسَة: Leadership, prominence, or desire to rule over others
